_what: Section 07: the argument over Planet Nine as a ledger, one row per paper, year by year. Lanes: for a planet, against one, data and searches (which may branch into a for/against row), and what comes next. Every title says what the result means for the search.
_caution: 'lane' and 'branch' are our editorial reading of what each paper does to the argument, like 'stance' in papers.json. Say so on the site.

Entries with a 'doi' take their title, authors, citation count and links from papers.json; 'title' and 'line' here are a one- or two-line retelling of that paper's abstract-checked summary, phrased as what it means for the search.
A 'branch' is drawn as its own for/against row under the data row, labelled as the finders' conclusion. Its title and line are the authors' own reading, from the abstract.
A branch with "of": "orbit" argues against the proposed orbit, not against a planet; the case against on the alternatives page leaves it out.
'excluded' percentages are the fractions of the predicted parameter space an empty search ruled out, quoted from the paper's abstract.
'diagram' names a drawing in src/charts/fieldart.js. The drawings are schematic: they show the kind of claim, not measured orbits.
'photos' are small inline portraits from Wikimedia Commons; scripts/fetch_portraits.py downloads them and fills in 'credit', 'license' and 'source' from the Commons API.
'next' entries describe searches that are under way or proposed. They are not findings.

_lanes.for: argues the pattern is real and a planet is the best explanation
_lanes.against: argues the pattern is a selection effect, or that something other than a planet explains it
_lanes.data: a new object, a constraint, a search or a survey; branches into a for/against row only when its authors draw that conclusion
_lanes.next: a search that is running or planned, and what it could settle

entries.title: A second object found too far out for Neptune to have put it there
entries.line: 2012 VP113 never comes within 80 AU of the Sun; only Sedna was known on such a remote orbit. Something else shaped these orbits, perhaps a passing star, the Sun's birth cluster or an unseen planet.

branch.title: Both remote orbits point the same way, and a hidden super-Earth could be why
branch.line: This suggestion was the seed of the Planet Nine idea.

entries.title: Nothing as big as Saturn lies within 28,000 AU
entries.line: NASA's WISE telescope swept the whole sky in infrared and found no large, warm companion to the Sun. What is left to look for is a planet a few times Earth's mass, cold and faint.

entries.title: Six aligned orbits point to a planet of ten Earth masses, Planet Nine
entries.line: Simulations show that a distant planet on an opposing orbit would herd the orbits into this alignment, and the authors name it Planet Nine.

photos.commons: File:Konstantin Batygin by Christopher Michel in 2022 01.jpg

entries.title: In some directions Saturn would have felt the planet's pull, so it cannot be there
entries.line: Cassini's ranging to Saturn is precise enough to sense a nearby massive planet's pull. Those directions come off the predicted orbit; the rest stays open.

entries.title: The longest orbits beat in simple ratios, a second route to the same planet
entries.line: Period ratios like these are what resonance with a planet near 665 AU would produce.

entries.title: The alignment may be an artefact of where telescopes happened to look
entries.line: OSSOS logged exactly where it pointed and how deep it saw. Its own eight distant objects are consistent with no clustering.

entries.title: A new extreme object, tilted 54 degrees out of the planets' plane
entries.line: 2015 BP519, from the Dark Energy Survey, has by one measure the most extreme orbit known, exactly the kind Planet Nine is predicted to produce.

branch.title: A tilt like this is what a distant massive planet would produce
branch.line: It would be the first of a predicted family of tilted orbits steered by the planet, adding to the circumstantial case.

entries.title: The distant bodies could align themselves, with no planet
entries.line: A swarm of small distant bodies with enough combined mass tilts and clusters itself.

entries.title: Correcting for the biases, the alignment is still a 1-in-500 fluke
entries.line: A model of how the surveys could have shaped the sample leaves the clustering standing. A review the same year shrinks the planet to 5 to 10 Earth masses on a closer orbit.

entries.title: Three bias-tracked surveys see no significant clustering at all
entries.line: 14 distant objects from DES, OSSOS and the Sheppard–Trujillo survey are consistent with random orientations. If the pattern is not there, there is nothing for a planet to explain.

entries.title: A refined orbit puts the planet at 6 Earth masses and about 380 AU, with a map of where to look
entries.line: The clustering stays at 99.6% significance, and the planet fits closer and brighter than first thought, within reach of large telescopes.

photos.commons: File:Konstantin Batygin by Christopher Michel in 2022 01.jpg

entries.title: A search for the planet's own heat finds nothing
entries.line: The Atacama Cosmology Telescope scanned almost half the sky at millimetre wavelengths, where a cold planet glows faintly. Ten weak candidates turned up, none convincing.

excluded.text: ruled out for a 5 Earth-mass planet (9% for 10)

diagram.note: for a planet of 5 Earth masses

entries.title: A direct search rules out half of the predicted planets
entries.line: Brown and Batygin comb the Zwicky Transient Facility's archive of photos for a slow-moving dot and find no candidate.

excluded.text: of the predicted planets ruled out

entries.title: Three-quarters of the predicted planets are now ruled out
entries.line: Nothing turns up in the Pan-STARRS1 photos either, which reach fainter. What is left is faint and near the Milky Way, the hardest place to search.

excluded.text: of the predicted planets ruled out, with ZTF and DES

diagram.note: with ZTF and the Dark Energy Survey

entries.title: One faint source may have moved the way Planet Nine would
entries.line: Two infrared surveys of the whole sky, IRAS in 1983 and AKARI in 2006, each recorded a source the other did not, a short way apart. If it is one object, it is a planet of 7 to 17 Earth masses, 500 to 700 AU out. Two sightings cannot fix an orbit, so it stays a candidate until a telescope finds it again.

branch.title: If real, a planet of 7 to 17 Earth masses, 500 to 700 AU out
branch.line: It stays a candidate until a telescope follows it up.

entries.title: A fourth Sedna-like object, on an orbit that does not fit the pattern
entries.line: 2023 KQ14, nicknamed Ammonite, found with the Subaru Telescope, never comes closer than 66 AU and stays stable over 4.5 billion years.

branch.title: Any planet must sit farther out
branch.line: Its orbit does not align with the other three, and its stability favours a large planet near 500 AU rather than a closer one.

entries.title: A likely dwarf planet, on the widest orbit of any
entries.line: 2017 OF201, about 700 km across, on an 830 AU orbit.

branch.title: Its orbit points away from the cluster
branch.line: The authors read this as a challenge to the evidence for a planet.

entries.title: The telescope most likely to find Planet Nine, or rule it out, starts work
entries.line: Rubin's ten-year survey reaches far fainter than the searches so far and will sweep much of the planet's predicted path again and again. It began on 29 June 2026 and has already found a probable dwarf planet, 2026 ED138.

links.label: SLAC: first dwarf planet candidate (27 Oct 2026)

entries.title: Within a few years, Rubin should either find the planet or empty most of what remains
entries.line: Most predicted brightnesses are within reach of a single Rubin image. A slow mover crossing successive images would give it away.

entries.title: A few deep images could confirm or kill the infrared candidates
entries.line: DECam or Subaru pointings along their predicted tracks would show whether they move like a planet.

entries.title: Listen for the planet's own heat with the Simons Observatory
entries.line: On ACT's plateau with far more sensitivity, a repeat of the millimetre search would not depend on how much sunlight the planet reflects.

entries.title: Every new distant orbit is a vote on whether the pattern is real
entries.line: Rubin should find tens of thousands of trans-Neptunian objects. If the new ones cluster, the case for a planet grows; if they scatter, it fades.
